description: We are building a CLPS Lunar Mission Browser using NASA data to visualize lunar landing sites, Sun/Earth visibility, power and communication windows, and mission timelines. We are interested in space, robotics, AI, and engineering software. We welcome teammates with skills in web development, 3D visualization, space data, backend, AI, robotics, or UI/UX.
summary: Launch dates slip. At the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so a slip of a few days can leave a good landing site in shadow or out of sight of Earth. Moonkeeper is a web tool for the question a mission planner has on that day: where do we land now, and when? It opens on the answer: a map of the south pole, computed from NASA LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons positions at 1.18 million ground points for 778 landing dates, lit where a 14-day mission keeps power and Earth in view. For 8 candidate sites it also checks that the approach path is lit. The windows are narrow: a 7-day slip breaks 559 of the 1,043 plans that passed, and 306 plans fail on the approach path alone. After a delay, Moonkeeper ranks two ways out, wait at the same site or land the same day somewhere else, and finds one for 554 of those 559. It then scatters 1,000 "ghost landers" around the target and reports the share that still meets the criteria. Pick a site and the map flies into a photograph that has not been taken yet: the site at the chosen hour, path traced from NASA terrain and the real direction of the Sun. Our Sun and Earth visibility agrees with NASA's PGDA illumination maps with an RMSE of 1.4 points for the Sun and 2.9 for Earth (r ≥ 0.99 at 150 random points). Live: nkm1020.github.io/moonkeeper
details:
Connecting Ridge CR1 at 04:00 UTC on 19 November 2026, 40 hours after a landing on 17 November. Path traced from NASA terrain with the Sun where JPL Horizons puts it. The headline is written from the data at that hour.

Who this is for, and why this problem

Our user is a mission planner at a lunar lander company in the week a launch slips. This is not a rare case. The challenge background names it directly: after a launch delay, teams must look again at other sites in the region, or at other dates for the same site.

At the south pole the cost of a slip is high. The Sun moves along the horizon, never far above it, and a ridge tens of kilometres away can hide it for days. Earth also sits low, so the direct radio link comes and goes. A site that was a good choice on the planned date can be a bad one a week later.

The 2025 IM-2 mission shows how fast a mission ends once power is gone. The lander came to rest on its side in a small crater near the south pole, could not recharge, and the mission ended in less than a day.

We also built for people who are not planners. A teacher or a student can open the sky screen and understand it with no training, because it is a photograph.

Our point of view

Most tools for this challenge answer one question: how good is this site on this date? We think a planner needs three other answers.

  • What now? Re-planning is the main output, not an extra. After a delay Moonkeeper shows that the old answer failed, why it failed, and what to do next, in ranked order.
  • Is the way down lit? A lander with optical navigation must see the ground it flies over. We check the approach path, not only the landing spot. NASA's 2024 Human Landing System update states that passive terrain navigation needs a lit approach.
  • How sure are we? No lander hits its target exactly. We test 1,000 landing points inside the landing error and report the share that still meets the criteria, with its interval, not a single yes or no.

And one rule for the interface: show the place, then the numbers. A planner must explain the choice to other people. A picture of the Sun going behind a named ridge is easier to explain than a table. The tool opens on the answer itself: a map of the south pole, computed at 1.18 million ground points for 778 landing dates, lit where a 14-day mission keeps power and Earth in view. Click any ground to read it; pick a site and the map flies into its photograph. Live: nkm1020.github.io/moonkeeper

What Moonkeeper does

  1. Sky. A simulated photograph of the site at any hour in the 30 days after landing: a live 3D view that turns into a path-traced frame when the view rests. A one-line headline written from the data, and a film strip of the whole month.
  2. Replan. A map of 8 sites × 792 landing dates. Enter the delay and get two ranked ways out: wait at the same site, or land the same day at another site.
  3. Confidence. 1,000 ghost landers spread inside the landing error. The share that keeps power, comms and a lit approach, with a 95% interval.
  4. Evidence. Which terrain hides the Sun, and how our numbers compare with NASA's maps.
  5. Decision. One card with the chosen site, date, margins, Plan B and confidence, with the data sources.

1 · The sky, as a photograph that has not been taken yet

The same hour at all eight sites, path traced, with the headline Moonkeeper writes for each.

The sky screen shows what a camera above the site would record at the chosen hour. The terrain is real. Near four sites it is NASA's photo-derived 5 m model, where small craters come from LRO photographs and not from interpolation. The Sun and Earth are where JPL Horizons puts them, and there is no other light.

The view has two layers. While the user moves through time, a live 3D view lights the ground by the same rule as our numbers: the share of the solar disc above each point's own horizon. When the view rests on a marked hour, it fades to a frame of the same terrain, the same Sun and the same camera, path traced in Blender Cycles. In that frame the faint light in the shade is real light reflected by the sunlit ground. We made 296 such frames for the eight sites.

The 30 days after landing at Connecting Ridge CR1, one line of pixels per hour.

Under the photograph is a month in one image. For each hour after landing the mast camera keeps one line of pixels through the Sun. Where the line of light breaks, a ridge is in front of the Sun. The headline above the photograph is written from the data at that hour, for example "The last hours of sunlight on Connecting Ridge CR1."

2 · Re-planning after a slip

8 sites × 792 landing dates. Green passes all three checks.

Only 1,055 of the 6,224 plans we can compute pass all three checks (the last 14 dates run past the end of the data). The pattern repeats with the lunar month, and it is different at every site. This is why a slip matters: the passing windows are narrow.

A worked example: a landing at the IM-2 site on 17 November 2026, seven days late.

A 7-day slip breaks 559 of the 1,043 plans that passed. A 3-day slip breaks 326 of 1,051, and a 1-day slip breaks 137 of 1,053. For 554 of the 559 broken plans Moonkeeper finds at least one passing alternative. For the other 5 it says so plainly: no safe alternative found, engineering review required.

The ranking rule is simple and stated on screen: passing candidates only, then the larger margin, then the shorter wait, then the shorter distance.

3 · The way down

306 of the 6,224 plans have power and comms at the landing spot but fail on the approach path alone. A tool that checks only the landing spot would call these days good. They are the solid pink columns in the map above.

We measure the approach as the share of ground under the descent path, from 0.5 to 10 km before the landing spot, where the Sun is above that ground's own horizon. We test 8 approach directions and keep the best one.

4 · Confidence

1,000 ghost landers around the IM-2 site, landing 5 February 2028.

On 5 February 2028 the IM-2 site passes at its centre, with a power margin of only 2%. With a 100 m landing error, 714 of 1,000 landers keep power and 286 do not. Each lander is tested against the terrain horizon of the nearest of 317 grid points, 80 m apart. The share that passes is 71% (95% interval 69–74%). The interval covers only the sampling noise of 1,000 landers, not the assumed criteria, the landing error or the terrain.

5 · A neural network that scouts

Neural Horizon Field against the precise calculation.

Testing thousands of points needs thousands of horizons, and a precise horizon is slow. During the event we trained a Neural Horizon Field. It is fast enough to search a wide area. It is not exact, so the final answer always comes from the precise calculation. We show both, and we show where they differ.

How it works

  1. Terrain to horizons. For each site we cast rays over the LOLA elevation models along great circles, with the Moon's curvature, out to the edge of the maps. The result is the terrain horizon in every direction, 2 m above the ground.
  2. Sun and Earth. JPL Horizons gives their direction from each site every hour from November 2026 to December 2028 (19,008 hours).
  3. Visibility. Sun: the share of the solar disc above the horizon. Earth: in view if any part of its disc is above the horizon, the same rule as NASA's maps.
  4. Window metrics. For each landing date and a 14-day mission: mean sunlight, longest dark period, share of time with Earth in view, longest gap without Earth, and approach lighting. The margin of a plan is its smallest margin.
  5. Plan B and ghost landers. Computed from the same metrics. Ghost landers use a fixed random seed and a Wilson score interval.
  6. The web. Everything is computed in advance and saved as JSON. The site is static and only draws the files. The browser makes no pass or fail decision.

Design choices. One colour per cause on every screen: power, comms and the approach each keep their own colour, always with the name next to it. All times in UTC, with KST next to them. English first, with a Korean switch. Every file carries its sources, its limits and its SI-use note in its metadata.

What we checked

Moonkeeper against NASA PGDA illumination maps at 150 random points.

  • Sun and Earth visibility. 150 random points from 85.2°S to the pole, chosen before any comparison, against NASA PGDA maps over 18.6 years. Sun: RMSE 1.4 percentage points, r = 0.996. Earth: RMSE 2.9 points, r = 0.990.
  • Neural horizons. The same 150 points and 317 grid points against the precise horizons. Mean error 0.10° on the grid, 0.16° on the 150 points.
  • Neural horizons in the decision. The same 1,000 ghost landers on all 97 passing dates of the IM-2 site. Within 5 points on all 83 safe dates. Lower by more than 10 points on 7 of the 14 risky dates; NHF is not always cautious (its horizon is slightly high on this grid and slightly low at the 150 points). Final verdicts use the precise horizon.
  • Ghost-lander sampling. 10 different random seeds. Spread 1.5 points; 1.4 expected for 1,000 samples.
  • 5 m terrain in the photographs. 5 m heights against the 40 m map at 7 sites. RMS 1.4 to 1.9 m.
  • Live view against path-traced frame. Same camera and hour at Connecting Ridge CR1, one on top of the other. Terrain and shadow edges fall on the same pixels.
  • Hourly Sun and Earth data. 6-hour data filled to 1 hour, against true 1-hour data. Difference below 0.000002°.

Limits and next steps

  • The thresholds are assumed. We found no public number for the minimum sunlight or the longest dark period a commercial lander can survive, so the five limits (50% mean sunlight, 96 h of dark, 40% Earth in view, 240 h gap, 0.5 approach) are demo values. They are in one file, and every result is labelled "assumed". Next step: take the limits from a real lander's power and thermal design.
  • Earth in view is not a radio link. We check geometry only. Next step: ground-station visibility and a link budget.
  • Terrain resolution. The decision uses 40 m and 80 m terrain. Rocks and small craters are below that. The photographs use 5 m terrain near seven sites (photo-derived at four) and 40 m at the IM-2 site.
  • Landing error. 100 m in both directions is an assumption. Next step: a real dispersion ellipse along the approach direction.
  • Approach lighting is a proxy. It counts lit ground under the path. It is not a navigation-camera simulation.
  • The photographs are simulated. The path-traced frames include light reflected by terrain within 60 km; the live view only estimates it. The ground is a rough diffuse surface, not a full regolith model. Path-traced frames exist for the first 3 to 5 days after one landing date. The label SIMULATED stays in the frame.

Tools

Python and NumPy for the calculation. PyTorch for the Neural Horizon Field. JavaScript modules, WebGL2 and three.js for the web. Blender Cycles for the path-traced frames. The JPL Horizons API. Google Colab and a GPU server for training. Figma for the interface design. GitHub and Notion for the team.

Use of SI

We used Claude (Anthropic), including Claude Code, for calculation code, web code, checks and drafts of this text. Team members set the direction, asked for each check and reviewed the results. Each data file has an "si_use" or "calc_si_usage" note in its metadata, and the repository README keeps an SI-use log per member. The Neural Horizon Field is our own model, designed and trained by the team during the event on horizons computed from NASA LOLA data; it is not a pre-trained or generative model.

No image or video in this project was made by a generative image model. The simulated photographs are computed from NASA terrain and JPL positions by our code, in the browser (WebGL) and in Blender Cycles (path tracing), and carry the word SIMULATED in the frame. Charts are plotted by code from our result files and say so in their footer. No NASA logo, flag or mission identifier appears in any of them.

Team

  • Kangmin: lead. Terrain horizons, Sun and Earth visibility, approach lighting, the sky screen and its 3D scenes.
  • Hyunjhee: re-planning map, Plan B candidates, ghost landers, validation against NASA maps.
  • Yonghwi: Neural Horizon Field: training, grid horizons, accuracy and speed checks.
  • Keev: decision rules for Plan B, research for the criteria and the landing error.
  • Chaewon: interface design: wireframes, design system, the five-screen flow.

All code, data files and figures: github.com/nkm1020/moonkeeper
